outcome: The infinitude of Fibonacci primes remains an open question; nothing since 26 January 2024 has resolved it or settled any restriction of it. Only record-extension activity (larger probable primes found) and a general heuristic paper touching Fibonacci-like recurrences (finalized/aligned with publication in 2024 but originally from 2023) were found, neither of which changes the status of the bullet.
summary: Wikipedia's 'Fibonacci prime' article (checked live, September 2026) still states plainly 'It is not known whether there are infinitely many Fibonacci primes,' and no source found anywhere contradicts this. Three lines of activity turned up in the search, none of which change the status of the question. (1) Record extensions: F_201107 (42,029 digits) remains the largest *proven* Fibonacci prime, verified by Maia Karpovich in September 2023 — before the window. Within the window, a larger *probable* prime (Miller-Rabin PRP, not proven) F_10367321 was found in August 2024, and a still larger one, F_11964299, was found by Ryan Propper in June 2025. Per DEEP_DIVE.md §3.1, a record extension is explicitly excluded from counting as progress on an infinitude question — it narrows where an answer could hide, not whether one exists — so these are noted but do not move the status. (2) A 2018/2020 preprint and journal article by Fengsui Liu, 'There are Infinitely Many Fibonacci Primes,' claims a proof via a 'recursive sieve method.' This predates the window by several years and, more importantly, has never been accepted by the mathematical community: it appears only in a non-selective journal (Global Journal of Science Frontier Research) and on ResearchGate, with no digestion by experts, and Wikipedia's own article — which would be expected to reflect a genuine resolution — still lists the question as open. There is no evidence this claim was newly evaluated, endorsed, or reopened within the window, so it does not create an event to date inside 2024-2026. (3) A 2023 paper by Jon Grantham and Andrew Granville, 'Fibonacci primes, primes of the form 2^n-k and beyond' (arXiv:2307.07894), gives a heuristic framework for primality in exponentially growing linear recurrence sequences (including Fibonacci-like sequences) but explicitly does not resolve finiteness vs infinitude — the authors state only a conjectural dichotomy. Its only within-window activity is a v3 revision (September 2024) that the authors describe as 'minor changes to align with the published version,' i.e., a journal-formatting update to a 2023 preprint, not new mathematical content, so it is not a distinct in-window event. No AI or LLM involvement was found in any of this activity — the primality records are computational (Miller-Rabin/GPU-style search by individual hobbyist-mathematicians), and the Grantham-Granville paper is standard human number theory with no disclosed AI use. Given all this, the status is 'open' with no_change_found true, matching the triage's 'none' verdict, which I confirm rather than contradict.
competing_reading: One could argue the Liu preprint deserves a 'claimed' status if reread charitably, since it explicitly claims a full proof of exactly this bullet's statement. I did not classify it that way because (a) it predates the window (2018/2020, well before 26 January 2024) so even if credited it would be open_stale rather than a live change, and (b) DEEP_DIVE.md requires that a 'claimed' status rest on some documented preprint/announcement/certificate that experts have not yet digested but that is at least being taken seriously; here there is no sign of even that — no citations engaging with its correctness, no digestion, and the Wikipedia article (checked live) still calls the question open years later, which is strong circumstantial evidence the claim was never found credible. I am confident 'open' is correct but note this as the closest call in the record.
what_would_settle_it: Any of: (a) a citation, review, or discussion by a recognized number theorist that seriously engages with Liu's claimed proof (either endorsing or refuting it) that I did not find; (b) a change to Wikipedia's Fibonacci prime or List of unsolved problems articles asserting resolution; (c) a new preprint post-January 2024 claiming a proof of infinitude that I did not encounter in these searches.
